									Read our review
									
							
$1699 at Apple										 | 
										$1699 at Best Buy US							
						


Mac mini M6 and M5 Pro specs
As well as the move from M4 and M4 Pro to M6 and M5 Pro, the Mac mini also gains storage that is up to twice as fast, according to Apple, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, 2.5Gb Ethernet. 
The M5 Pro model adds genlock support through its Thunderbolt 5 ports, for synchronizing a display and camera in professional video workflows.

				
					

				
			
The new M6 chip has launched in the Mac mini. 

Apple




Processor: M6 and M5 Pro chip compared
There may be some confusion over the chip generations in the new Mac mini. The mainstream model uses the newer M6 chip, while the more powerful model uses the older-generation M5 Pro. Pro chips are designed for heavier professional workloads, with more CPU and GPU cores, higher memory bandwidth, support for more unified memory, additional displays and faster Thunderbolt connectivity. So while M5 Pro remains the more capable chip overall, the M6 offers a significant step up from the M4 it replaces in the previous generation Mac mini. Macwelt has now tested the M6 Mac mini, and we have reviewed the M5 Pro Mac mini. Macwelt’s tests show that the M6 can lead in single-core CPU and Neural Engine performance, while the M5 Pro retains a clear advantage in multicore CPU and GPU performance.
M6: The Mac mini is the first Mac to ship with the M6 chip, replacing the M4 in the entry-level model. It features a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, up from 10 CPU and GPU cores in the previous generation, and supports up 170GB/s memory bandwidth if you choose 24GB or 32GB memory (the 16GB configuration offers 153GB/s bandwidth). Apple promises up to 40% faster CPU performance, twice the graphics performance and up to 4x faster AI performance than M4. It also introduces Apple’s first Dual 16-core Neural Engine, delivering up to twice the Neural Engine performance.
M5 Pro: The M5 Pro replaces the M4 Pro in the higher-end Mac mini and can be configured with up to an 18-core CPU and 20-core GPU. Apple claims up to 4x faster LLM processing, 1.4x faster Blender ray-tracing performance and 1.5x faster Affinity image processing than M4 Pro. It supports up to 64GB of unified memory with 307GB/s memory bandwidth. Both chips feature Neural Accelerators in their GPU cores, but the M5 Pro’s additional CPU and GPU cores, greater memory capacity and higher bandwidth make it better suited to video production, 3D rendering, development and larger local AI models.
What the benchmarks show
Macwelt tested an M6 Mac mini with 24GB of memory and a 512GB SSD. In Geekbench 7, it scored 4,055 in single-core and 22,695 in multicore, compared with 3,277 and 15,693 for Macwelt’s M4 mini. In the same set of tests, the M6 scored higher than the M5 Pro in single-core performance (4,055 versus 3,720), but the M5 Pro led by a substantial margin in multicore performance (34,281 versus 22,695) and GPU compute. That makes the M6 a compelling choice for most buyers, while the M5 Pro better suits heavily threaded and GPU-intensive work. These are results from the configurations tested, not measurements of the base M6 or M5 Pro models.


						

							


Storage 
Apple claims up to twice the storage performance of the previous generation. In Macwelt’s Blackmagic Disk Speed Test, its M6 mini with a 512GB SSD reached approximately 6,700MB/s writing and 6,400MB/s reading, versus 3,000MB/s writing and 3,400MB/s reading on its M4 comparison machine. SSD speed can vary by capacity, so these figures may not apply to the base 256GB M6 mini.
There is a downside to the new storage design. As our report explains, Expand Mac mini’s teardown found that both the M6 and M5 Pro models have NAND storage soldered to the logic board, replacing the removable modules used in the M4 and M4 Pro. This means that, unlike the M4 and M4 Pro, the new models cannot accept a replacement internal SSD module. You can still add storage by connecting an external SSD through USB-C or Thunderbolt. 
The base 256GB M6 also uses a single NAND package rather than the dual arrangement reported for the 512GB model, potentially limiting storage performance. 
Other than that the storage capacities are as before – 256GB,  512GB, 1TB and 2TB for the M6 model and 512GB, 1TB, 2TB, 4TB and 8TB SSDs for the M5 Pro model. 


						

							


RAM
Both the M4 and M6 Mac mini can be configured with up to 32GB of unified memory. 
Both the M4 Pro and M5 Pro models can be configured with up to 64GB.


						

							


Connectivity: WiFi & Bluetooth

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary / Foundry




Wi-Fi: Both models now support Wi-Fi 7 which replaces the previous wireless standard Wi-Fi 6E.
Bluetooth: Both models also move to Bluetooth 6, replacing Bluetooth 5.3.
Ethernet: Previously faster Ethernet was an upgrade; the new models now have 2.5Gb Ethernet, with 10Gb Ethernet available as a configurable option.
Thunderbolt: The M6 Mac mini has three Thunderbolt 4 ports and the the M5 Pro version has three Thunderbolt 5 ports. This is the same as the previous generation.
Genlock: Apple has added Genlock support over USB-C. This is used for synchronising a display and camera (which can be an iPhone 17 Pro). It is aimed at professional video workflows
Display support: The M6 Mac mini will support up to two 6K displays plus one 5K display, while the M5 Pro supports up to three 6K displays. 
Other ports include two USB-C/USB 3 ports and a headphone jack on the front and HDMI and Ethernet remain on the rear, as previously.

Who is the Mac mini best for?
The M6 Mac mini is the best fit for most buyers who want a fast, compact desktop for everyday work, coding and mainstream creative tasks. Macwelt’s tests show a substantial performance gain over the M4, although its test machine had 24GB of memory and a 512GB SSD rather than the base configuration.
Choose the M5 Pro Mac mini if your work benefits from its stronger multicore CPU and GPU performance, Thunderbolt 5, greater memory bandwidth or support for more than 32GB of unified memory. Those advantages are most relevant to sustained professional work and larger local AI models.
Check the price of the configuration you need before ordering: the M5 Pro starts at $1,699/£1,699, and memory, storage and other upgrades add up quickly. Our reviewed $2,899 M5 Pro mini cost $100 more than an M5 Max Mac Studio configuration with a stronger GPU and more ports, although the Studio had 36GB of memory rather than the mini’s 48GB. See our Mac mini buying guide for advice on which model to choose and whether to wait.


						

							


Should you buy the 2026 Mac mini?
The M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini are on sale now, and independent test results are available for both models. For advice on which configuration to choose, whether to buy now or wait for a discount, and how they compare with older models, read our Mac mini buying guide

title: Your $1,500 iPhone 18 Pro Max doesn’t need a case, honest!
content:
Macworld





I’ve never dropped a smartphone in my life. Ever. I’ve grown so confident that these days I use my iPhone without a case and screen protector at all times, since the chances of disaster are clearly low. But that doesn’t mean my phones live a completely charmed life.
After months of daily use, even without a drop, the display tends to attract micro scratches, while some degree of battery degradation is almost inevitable. It’s all part of the natural wear and tear that serves as a reminder that even premium hardware is ultimately a consumable.
The iPhone 17 Pro launched with a ton of fundamental changes to its internal and external designs back in September 2025. We got a new set of build materials, second-generation Ceramic Shield, a larger battery, improved thermal management, and much more. These modifications have noticeably impacted the iPhone’s durability—both positively and negatively. Having used an iPhone 17 Pro Max without protection since day one, I’m ready to evaluate how this latest flagship holds up.
Even though I was using an iPhone 17 Pro for this article, the conclusions apply to the iPhone 18 Pro, which has the same aluminum body and Ceramic Shield glass. In fact, when I traded in my iPhone 17 Pro Max last week to upgrade to the new model, the salesclerk could not believe it had been used for a full year without any form of protection. After thorough inspection of the display and back, he could only spot the smallest of blemishes.
More chipping, less cracking
While Pro iPhones have always featured the iconic triple-camera layout, their build materials have shifted over the years. The iPhone 11 Pro debuted with a stainless steel frame, a standard that held for the next three models. Although this construction generally didn’t chip, it did attract obvious scuffs and fingerprint smudges. With the iPhone 15 Pro and 16 Pro, Apple switched to a titanium alloy, which made the frame tougher and less prone to scratches. Then the iPhone 17 Pro came along, retiring titanium in favor of aluminum.
Aluminum is weaker than titanium, making the latest iPhone more susceptible to dents if dropped. I haven’t dropped mine to confirm, but it’s basic science. More importantly, the frame now chips easily with regular use—something I’ve never experienced with previous Pro iPhones I’ve owned. Even though I don’t use the Camera Control button, the aluminum around it has become nicked. The sharp, raised edge of the Pro camera system area has similarly chipped, revealing the silver metal beneath the blue finish.
Other design concerns include the small gap between the metal frame and back glass panel, which actively collects dust particles. That’s not to mention that the glass panel itself leaves visible marks when I attach a MagSafe charger, requiring me to rigorously polish it to restore the shine.
Looking at the bigger picture, minimizing the use of glass has made the iPhone’s back more durable. Unlike with previous models, a drop would now chip or bend the aluminum instead of cracking the expensive glass sheet. The iPhone 17 Pro’s aesthetics may not age as gracefully, but it’s certainly a more functional phone now.

				
					

				
			The Camera Control button showed some nicks around the edge.
Mahmoud Itani / Foundry




The toughest screen yet 
The durability of the screen is arguably more significant than that of any other component; it’s the part you’ll be viewing and interacting with, and any imperfections to its smooth surface will be distractingly obvious. With this in mind I always place my iPhone in a separate pocket on its own, away from keys and other sharp objects. I also avoid putting it face down on solid surfaces such as restaurant tables. For years, this approach has protected my iPhone’s screen from big scratches—but there was no escaping the micro abrasions that are particularly noticeable in direct sunlight after months of regular use.
At the iPhone 17 launch event, Apple boasted about the display’s Ceramic Shield 2, which supposedly triples its scratch resistance. I initially dismissed this marketing lingo, as upgrading my iPhone annually typically makes it hard to notice these types of iterative introductions. Boy, was I wrong.
After seven months of use without a screen protector, my iPhone 17 Pro Max’s display has zero micro scratches. This is the first time in my life I’ve managed to use a smartphone this long without the screen developing any sort of surface damage. I haven’t changed the way I handle it; the Ceramic Shield 2 is just that much better at resisting scratches, maintaining the phone’s pristine look.
To avoid any chipping, nicking, scratching, and shattering, take a look at Macworld’s reviews of the best cases for iPhone 18 Pro series.

				
					

				
			Spot the scratch. You may be looking for a while.
Mahmoud Itani / Foundry




Better thermals, less battery degradation
Beyond the cosmetics, the battery plays a major role when evaluating a smartphone’s durability. I typically connect my iPhone to a wired charger when its battery level drops to 20 percent and disconnect it right after it reaches 100 percent. I occasionally rely on a MagSafe charger and leave it plugged in overnight without enabling any optimized battery charging features. Within 6 months, the battery’s maximum capacity would usually drop to 95 percent or so.
With the iPhone 17 Pro, Apple introduced an aluminum build and vapor chamber for improved thermal management, along with a larger battery. (The 18 Pro brings a a next-generation vapor chamber with a new design built for improves sustained performance.) These changes minimize overheating and stretch the flagship’s battery life remarkably, slowing down the degradation cycle. While I still follow the same charging and usage routines, my iPhone 17 Pro Max’s maximum battery capacity stayed near 100 percent longer than ever, and the 18 Pro should do event better. So users holding on to their iPhones for multiple years won’t need to have the batteries replaced as often.

				
					

				
			Battery health degrades more slowly than in the past.
Mahmoud Itani / Foundry




Conclusions: Amazingly durable, with room for improvement
This wasn’t the perfect performance across the board, and Apple has left room for improvement in future generations. This isn’t unusual: radically transformed products are often riddled with imperfections that manufacturers address in the years that follow. The MacBook Air M3, for example, added an anodization seal to minimize fingerprints on the Midnight variant following M2 user complaints. Apple could similarly tweak the iPhone’s aluminum coating to limit chipping. The back glass panel on the iPhone 18 Pro is now color-matched to the body, but it has the same Ceramic Shield scratch resistance rather than the 2nd-gen process used on the front glass.
As for the display’s resistance, I’m genuinely impressed by how the Ceramic Shield 2 is holding up: 10 out of 10, no notes. The battery life and thermal management have likewise become more reliable than ever. At this point, any groundbreaking changes to the battery will probably require dropping the lithium-ion technology in favor of something completely different. Once a fragile glass sandwich, the iPhone Pro has become a beacon of durability and dependability.

title: Best Mac 2026: Every Apple Mac and MacBook compared
content:
Macworld






Which Mac is best for you? 
Whether you want everyday portability, professional creative power, desktop performance, or budget-friendly computing, Apple’s lineup has a Mac that fits. For $699 you can own a MacBook Neo, which is Apple’s most affordable laptop. Spend a little more and the MacBook Air excels at everyday work and battery life, while the MacBook Pro lineup delivers the extra power required by demanding professional workloads. If you prefer a desktop, the iMac is a great all-in-one option for the home, while Mac mini offers good value if you don’t need portability and already have a display and accessories. At the top end, the Mac Studio is built for intensive professional workloads, including demanding creative work and AI development.
Choosing the best Mac in 2026 isn’t simply about buying the newest model; it’s about finding the Mac that best matches what you need from a computer. Apple’s lineup ranges from ultraportable MacBooks to powerful desktop Macs, with options for students, everyday users, creatives and professionals.
In this Mac buying guide, we cover everything you need to know about the MacBook Neo, MacBook Air, MacBook Pro, Mac mini, iMac and Mac Studio, including the differences in size, specs, features and price. We’ll help you decide which Mac and configuration offers the right balance of value, performance and portability for you.
Best Mac 2026: Mac & MacBook Buyers Guide
Our top Mac for most people in 2026 is the MacBook Air. It offers an excellent combination of performance, portability and value in a compact package that will suit the typical Mac user.
If you need more power, we recommend the MacBook Pro, which delivers high-end performance in a portable form. At the other end of the price range, the new MacBook Neo starts at $699/£699 and is Apple’s most affordable Mac laptop.
If you don’t need a laptop, Apple also has some excellent desktop options. The Mac Studio offers exceptional performance for the money and can save thousands compared with a similarly specified Mac laptop, while the Mac mini is Apple’s cheapest desktop Mac, starting at $899/£899.
Below, we take you through every Mac currently available from Apple, explaining who each model is best suited to and what you should consider when choosing a configuration. You’ll also find live prices to help you find the best deal today. For more help choosing between Apple’s laptops, see our MacBook comparison.
Price increases June 2026
In June 2026, Apple increased prices significantly across several product lines including Macs, iPads, the Apple TV 4K, and HomePod models, citing an unprecedented rise in component costs. 
The company stated it had “never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly” and that it had shielded customers from these increases for as long as possible before finally raising prices.

What is it? The 13-inch MacBook Air is Apple’s thin and light laptop for everyday use, offering more performance and features than the cheaper MacBook Neo.
What’s new? Apple introduced the M5 MacBook Air in March 2026, featuring the M5 chip with its faster CPU and GPU. The base configuration now starts with 512GB of storage (double the previous model), along with faster SSD speeds, more memory bandwidth, and support for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.
Who’s it for? It’s perfect for students and everyday users who want a lightweight laptop that’s easy to carry, and powerful enough for working, studying, browsing, and doing light creative work. If you want a larger screen there is a 15-inch MacBook Air, which we discuss below. 
How much does the 13-inch MacBook Air cost? The entry-level 13-inch M5 MacBook Air costs from $1,299/£1,299, that’s up $200/£200 from the launch price of $1,099/£1,099. You can create build-to-order models with more memory (up to 32GB) or storage (up to 4TB).
What are the specifications? The standard specs for the M5 MacBook Air offer an improvement compared to the previous generation. The MacBook Air now ships with 512GB SSD as standard. 
Apple M5, 10-core CPU, 8-core GPU, 16GB memory, 512GB SSD, two Thunderbolt 4 ports: $1,299/£1,299.
Apple M5, 10-core CPU, 10-core GPU, 16GB memory, 512GB SSD, two Thunderbolt 4 ports: $1,399/£1,399.
Additional options: Up to 32GB memory, 4TB storage.
What are display specifications? 
While referred to as 13-inch, when measured diagonally the screen is 13.6-inches.
The 13.6-inch Liquid Retina on the M5 MacBook Air display has a native resolution of 2,560×1,664 and 500 nits brightness.
The MacBook Air M5 can support two external displays.
How do I connect stuff? The M5 MacBook Air models supports Thunderbolt 4, which means that they can support a dual monitor set up. If you want to connect USB-A devices, you need either a USB-C to USB-A adapter, like Apple’s $19 / £19 one, or a USB-C hub that has USB-A ports. In the U.K. and Europe Apple has stopped including a Power Adapter in the box, so you will need to buy one separately. See our round-up of the best USB-C hubs and adapters.
The 2026 MacBook Air offers Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) for connecting to a network. It also provides built-in Bluetooth (6) for wirelessly connecting a mouse or other peripherals. If you want to connect to an ethernet network, you need an adapter.
How fast is it? In our tests the M5 saw consistent gains over the M4 in the previous generation, as you can see in our Mac processor benchmarks. In some benchmarks the M5 even beats the M1 Ultra. If you are upgrading from an old Mac – especially if it is one with an Intel chip – you will see a huge difference.
Any other considerations? The MacBook Air should be more than fast enough for general-purpose use. The only issue is that, because it doesn’t have an internal fan, it may slow down during long processing sessions to keep cool. So if you are likely to be video editing or compiling code the MacBook Pro with its fan is a better choice. Also note that it’s impossible to upgrade the storage or memory after purchase, so you should buy the model with the largest amount of storage and memory you can afford or invest in external storage. 
Why we recommend the 13-inch MacBook Air: The MacBook Air is a great choice for someone who does general-purpose work and moves around a lot, such as a student or a self-employed person.

What is it? The M6 Mac mini is Apple’s smallest and most affordable desktop Mac. It has the same compact 5×5-inch design introduced with the M4 Mac mini in 2024, but the M6 replaces the M4 chip inside. Unlike an iMac, the Mac mini doesn’t include a display, keyboard or mouse, so it is particularly attractive if you already own those things. Note that while M5 Pro name indicates that the chip is an older generaion, it is still considerably more powerful  than the M6.
What’s new? Apple updated the Mac mini with the M6 chip in August 2026, on-sale from September 22. The design hasn’t changed, but there are some significant improvements inside. The M6 has a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, up from 10 CPU and GPU cores in the M4, along with Neural Accelerators in every GPU core and Apple’s first Dual 16-core Neural Engine. Maximum unified memory increases from 24GB to 32GB and memory bandwidth rises from 120GB/s on the M4 to as much as 170GB/s. Apple also says storage is up to twice as fast. Connectivity has been upgraded with Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and 2.5Gb Ethernet as standard.
Who’s it for? The M6 Mac mini is a good choice for anyone who wants a powerful desktop Mac but doesn’t need the additional performance of the M5 Pro Mac mini or Mac Studio. It has more than enough power for everyday work, web browsing and office apps, but is also capable of photo and video editing, coding and gaming. Apple is particularly pushing the M6 Mac mini for AI workloads, including running local AI models and AI agents. If your work involves demanding video production, 3D rendering, large AI models or other processor-intensive professional workflows, the M5 Pro version will be a better choice.
How much does the Mac mini cost? The M6 Mac mini starts at $899/£899 with 16GB unified memory and a 256GB SSD. That’s $100/£100 more than the M4 Mac mini cost immediately before it was replaced, and $300/£300 more than the M4 model’s original $599/£599 launch price in October 2024. A 16GB model with 512GB storage costs $1,199/£1,199. There is also an M6 configuration with 24GB memory and 512GB storage, while additional memory and storage upgrades can be selected when you order.

The Mac mini does not include a display, keyboard, or mouse, so you’ll have to provide your own, or you can customize your order to include these devices as extra-cost options.
How do I connect stuff? There are two USB-C ports on the front of the Mac mini, supporting USB 3 at up to 10Gb/s, alongside a 3.5mm headphone jack. On the back are three Thunderbolt 4/USB-C ports capable of speeds up to 40Gb/s, an HDMI port and a 2.5Gb Ethernet port. The Ethernet connection can be upgraded to 10Gb when you order. Wireless connectivity has also been upgraded to Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, and the Mac mini includes Thread networking support. The M6 model can drive as many as three displays, including two 6K screens and a third 5K display. Unlike some older Mac mini models, there are no USB-A ports, so you’ll need an adapter or hub for older USB accessories.
How fast is it?  In Macwelt’s tests of an M6 Mac mini with 24GB of memory and a 512GB SSD, Geekbench 7 single-core performance rose from 3,277 on the M4 mini to 4,055, while multicore rose from 15,693 to 22,695. GPU compute was roughly 70–80 percent higher in its Geekbench 7 and Cinebench 2024 tests. Gaming improved too, although the demanding Steel Nomad test still produced a low frame rate. The M6 is a strong choice for everyday work and moderately demanding creative tasks; sustained GPU-heavy work and larger local AI models are reasons to consider the M5 Pro.
Any other considerations? The base 256GB model also uses a single NAND storage package, which could limit SSD speeds compared with the 512GB model’s reported dual-package design, although we don’t yet have benchmarks establishing the difference. Read more about the Mac mini’s storage changes. If you need more memory, Thunderbolt 5, or stronger multicore CPU and GPU performance for demanding workloads, look at the M5 Pro Mac mini instead. What’s best, MacBook Air or MacBook Pro?
We address this question in detail in our comparison of the MacBook Air vs Pro. It’s really a question of price versus power. The Air is sufficient for most people’s needs, the Pro will give you that extra boost in terms of what the Mac is capable of.
Buying an entry-level MacBook Air for $1,299/£1,299 will get you an excellent Mac laptop. If you want to spend less than that you may be able to find a discounted MacBook Air – we round up the best MacBook Air deals regularly.
If you want a larger screen, the 15-inch MacBook Air is a great option that is a lot cheaper than the smaller 14-inch MacBook Pro. 
The price of the Pro and Max MacBook Pro models is high, but these models offer the kind of specs professional users, especially creatives, need, including support for more RAM, and more CPU and GPU cores. If you can afford to stretch to the Max you will get the ultimate Mac without a doubt, but you need to be willing to make a significant investment.
The choice between the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro is all down to the screen size. The 16-inch models are more expensive, but once you spec them out in such a way to be comparable the price difference is minor. The bigger difference is between the Pro and Max processors. Other than speed, MacBooks with Max processors can connect up to four external displays (three over Thunderbolt and one over HDMI), while since the M4 all models allow two external displays in addition to the laptop screen. (There are workarounds if you need to connect more screens).
There is now another Mac laptop to consider, the MacBook Neo lowers the price of ownership of a Mac laptop to $699/£699. If budget really is tight though, you might want to consider a discounted previous generation MacBook Air instead.





2.
Should I upgrade from my Intel Mac?
Yes. It’s time! We are now more than six years into Apple’s transition from Intel processors to its own silicon that includes CPU, GPU, and unified memory. The transition began with the introduction of the M1 in November 2020. Since June 2023 every Mac Apple sells uses Apple’s own chips rather than Intel processors.
If you’ve yet to upgrade your Intel Mac to one powered by Apple’s silicon what are you waiting for? If you are concerned that a must-have app doesn’t run on an M-series Mac, consider finding a new app because the performance gains are tremendous.
Another good reason to replace an Intel Mac is that Apple’s support for these models is winding down. macOS Golden Gate, released in September 2026, is the first major version of macOS to support no Intel Macs. Intel Macs compatible with older versions of macOS may continue receiving security updates for a limited period, but they are now outside Apple’s current feature-release cycle. Apple does not guarantee how long those updates will continue, and machines limited to macOS Sequoia are likely to lose support sooner than those capable of running macOS Tahoe. 4.
What specs do I really need for my Mac?
Chip: The specs you need depend on what you plan to do with your Mac. For everyday tasks such as web browsing, email, office apps and light photo editing, a standard M-series chip is more than sufficient. Apple’s latest entry-level desktop chip is the M6, available in the Mac mini, while other Macs still use M4 or M5-generation chips. 
If you regularly work with complex spreadsheets, large Photoshop files, audio projects, video editing or more demanding games, look at a Pro chip. The M5 Pro Mac mini, for example, offers up to an 18-core CPU and 20-core GPU and up to 64GB unified memory.
For professional video production, 3D work, software development and other intensive workloads, a Max chip is more appropriate. The Mac Studio with M5 Max offers an 18-core CPU, up to a 40-core GPU and as much as 128GB unified memory. 
The M5 Ultra, with up to a 36-core CPU, 80-core GPU and 512GB unified memory, is aimed at the most extreme workloads, including VFX, scientific computing and running very large AI models locally.
GPU: One of the biggest differences between Apple’s chips is GPU performance. Standard M-series chips are easily sufficient for everyday graphics, casual gaming and light creative work. Pro chips add considerably more GPU power for video editing, graphics work, 3D applications and gaming. Max chips are designed for professional graphics, high-resolution video and demanding 3D workflows, while Ultra provides Apple’s highest GPU performance. The M5 Max offers up to 40 GPU cores, while the M5 Ultra doubles that to 80 GPU cores. Both also have Neural Accelerators built into every GPU core to speed up AI workloads.
RAM: Apple calls RAM Unified Memory. The MacBook Neo is limited to 8GB, which is probably the biggest drawback of that machine. Most Macs start with at least 16GB, which is plenty for everyday use, although we recommend choosing more if your budget allows because the memory cannot be upgraded later. 24GB or 32GB is a good choice for heavier multitasking, photo editing, podcasting, moderate video production and gaming. Developers and professional creative users may benefit from 48GB, 64GB or more. The new M5 Pro Mac mini can be configured with up to 64GB, M5 Max Mac Studio with up to 128GB, and M5 Ultra Mac Studio with an enormous 512GB.
Storage: Even with iCloud and external drives available, it can seem like you can never have enough storage inside your Mac. 256GB may be sufficient for basic web and office use, but it can fill up quickly. We recommend 512GB for most people who want to keep a Mac for several years, particularly if you store photos, games or media locally. For regular video or audio production, 1TB or more is preferable. Professional users may need several terabytes: the M5 Pro Mac mini can be configured with up to 8TB, while Mac Studio configurations go even higher. As with unified memory, internal Mac storage cannot be upgraded after purchase, so it is worth thinking about future requirements when ordering.
For more information to help you decide which Mac to buy see our Mac processor comparison where we compare Apple silicon and Intel. We also offer advice about how much storage, RAM, and cores in How much MacBook RAM, SSD, GPU, and CPU do you really need.





5.
When were the Macs last updated?
In August 2026 the Mac mini and Mac Studio were updated. 
In March 2026 the MacBook Pro and MacBook Air were updated, and the MacBook Neo was introduced.
The most recent iMac update was in October 2024.
The Mac Pro has been discontinued. 





Why you can trust Macworld’s advice
Macworld has been covering everything Apple related since our first issue which arrived alongside the original Mac in 1984. Nobody knows Apple better, except probably Apple, but the difference is that we are completely impartial. We are made up of a team of experts with decades of experiences with Macs and other Apple products, and between us we have reviewed every Apple product meaning we are uniquely positioned to provide buying advice.

title: Should you buy a Mac mini now? M6 vs M5 Pro buying advice
content:
Macworld





Apple announced the new M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini on August 25 and it started shipping on September 22, 2026.  For most buyers, we recommend the M6 Mac mini. Starting at $899/£899 – up from $599 for the M4 generation – it offers improved performance for everyday work, coding and creative tasks. It is particularly appealing if you already own a monitor, keyboard and mouse, or are replacing an Intel Mac or early Apple silicon model.
The M5 Pro Mac mini is aimed at more demanding users. Its stronger multicore CPU and GPU, Thunderbolt 5, greater memory bandwidth and support for up to 64GB of unified memory make it better for professional creative work, development and larger local AI models. However, prices start at $1,699/£1,699 and rise quickly with upgrades.
We now have independent tests of both models. Our colleagues at Macwelt found that its M6 Mac mini was substantially faster than the M4, while our M5 Pro review found strong performance gains but questioned its value at the higher price. We discuss what those results mean for your choice below.
This guide explains whether to buy now, which model to choose, how much to pay, and the alternatives, drawbacks and refurbished options to consider.


Should you buy a Mac mini now? 
It’s a good time to buy a Mac mini. With another significant update unlikely soon, there is little reason to wait if you need a compact desktop Mac.
If you were waiting to see independent benchmarks, we have tested the Mac mini M5 Pro and our German sister title Macwelt has reviewed the Mac mini M6, so we have the data that will help you make your decision.
There are reasons to wait though. Discounts are likely to improve in the months after launch, particularly around Prime Day in October and Black Friday in November, and more refurbished or discounted M4 models may appear as buyers upgrade. If you’re happy with your current Mac or simply want the lowest possible price, there is no need to rush. 
You may prefer not to risk waiting. A global memory shortage contributed to long delivery times and limited availability for the previous generation, and similar supply constraints could affect the new models. The higher cost of memory and other components has also contributed to the Mac mini’s substantial price increase.
Buy Mac mini now if:
You need a Mac mini now and want the latest model.
You’re replacing an Intel Mac or an older Apple silicon Mac.
You want a powerful compact desktop for everyday, office, development or creative work.
The $899/£899 M6 Mac mini provides all the performance you need.
Consider M5 Pro if:
You need more than 32GB of unified memory.
You run demanding professional creative or development workloads.
You want to run larger local AI or LLM workloads.
You need Thunderbolt 5 or substantially greater memory bandwidth.
Wait if: 
You’re hoping for discounts around Prime Day or Black Friday.
Your current Mac still meets your needs.
You don’t need a new Mac urgently and want to see whether prices fall.
Consider refurbished if:
You can find an M4 Mac mini at a significant discount.
You want the best value rather than the newest chip.
An Apple-refurbished M4 or M4 Pro configuration meets your memory and storage needs.
You’re comfortable waiting for refurbished M6 or M5 Pro stock to appear.  


						

							




		
Apple Mac mini (M6, 2026)
$879.99 at Amazon										 | 
										$899 at Apple										 | 
										$899 at Best Buy US							
						
Apple Mac mini (M5 Pro, 2026)

										
									Read our review
									
							
$1699 at Apple										 | 
										$1699 at Best Buy US							
						


Which Mac mini to buy: M6 or M5 Pro? 

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The Mac mini lineup has changed significantly in 2026, with Apple introducing the M6 and M5 Pro models in August. The choice between them comes down to your workload and budget, as they serve very different audiences despite sharing the same compact design.
Apple sells two Mac mini models, both announced on August 25 and shipping from September 22, 2026:
Mac mini (M6) — starts at $899 / £899
12-core CPU, 12-core GPU
16GB unified memory (up to 32GB)
Up to 2TB SSD
Thunderbolt 4 (three ports), two front USB-C ports, HDMI, 2.5Gb Ethernet (10Gb Ethernet optional)
Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread
Supports up to three displays (two 6K + one 5K)
Mac mini (M5 Pro) — starts at $1,699 / £1,699
15-core CPU, 16-core GPU (upgradeable to 18-core CPU, 20-core GPU for +$200)
24GB unified memory (up to 64GB)
Up to 8TB SSD
Thunderbolt 5 (three ports), two front USB-C ports, HDMI, 2.5Gb Ethernet (10Gb Ethernet optional)
Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread 
Supports up to three 6K displays
Despite its older generation number, the M5 Pro is the stronger choice for heavily threaded CPU and GPU work. It has more CPU and GPU cores, supports up to 64GB of unified memory rather than the M6’s 32GB, and offers 307GB/s of memory bandwidth compared with 153GB/s or 170GB/s for the M6, depending on its memory configuration. It also has Thunderbolt 5. However, the M6 was faster in Macwelt’s single-core CPU and quantized Neural Engine test, so the better choice depends on your workload.
Choose the M6 Mac mini if:
You don’t need more than 32GB of unified memory (RAM).
You need a compact, powerful desktop for everyday use – web browsing, office work, photo editing, coding, and general productivity.
You’re a student or budget-conscious buyer looking for the best-value option for home offices, school or office use. Education pricing brings the starting price down to $799.
You already own a monitor, keyboard, and mouse.
You don’t need the extra performance or connectivity of the M5 Pro model.
Choose the M5 Pro Mac mini if:
You’re a developer, video editor, 3D artist, musician, or researcher who needs sustained performance for demanding workloads.
You want to run larger local AI models. The M5 Pro’s higher memory ceiling and much greater memory bandwidth make it better suited to heavier LLM workloads than the M6. If local AI is a priority, choose your memory carefully because it cannot be upgraded later.
You need Thunderbolt 5 for faster external storage, high-bandwidth peripherals or professional video workflows.
You regularly work with heavy 3D rendering, high-end video production, large codebases or scientific workloads.
You need more than 32GB of unified memory.


						

							









							




M6 versus M5 Pro comparison


M6 Mac miniM5 Pro Mac mini

Best forEveryday work, coding and mainstream creative workSustained professional and AI workloads
Starting price$899/£899$1,699/£1,699
Memory16GB–32GB24GB–64GB
Memory bandwidth153GB/s or 170GB/s307GB/s
StorageUp to 2TBUp to 8TB
ThunderboltThunderbolt 4Thunderbolt 5
DisplaysTwo 6K plus one 5KThree 6K
Our verdictBest choice for most peopleBuy only if your workload requires it

 






Should you upgrade from an M4 or M4 Pro Mac mini?
Upgrade from an M4 Mac mini? The M6 is a substantial performance upgrade. In Macwelt’s tests, its 24GB/512GB M6 mini scored about 24 percent higher in Geekbench 7 single-core and 45 percent higher in multicore than the M4, with much larger gains in some GPU tests. But if your M4 already handles your work comfortably, those results alone are not a reason to replace it. Consider upgrading if its performance is holding up your work, or if you specifically need Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 or standard 2.5Gb Ethernet.
Upgrade from an M4 Pro Mac mini? The M5 Pro is faster, particularly in multicore work, but it is an expensive upgrade from a recent machine. In our tests of an upgraded M5 Pro mini, Geekbench 7 single-core performance improved by 12 percent, multicore by 38 percent and GPU compute by around 20 percent over the tested M4 Pro. Our review concluded that the higher price makes upgrading difficult to justify unless the time saved in your workload matters to you.


						

							


How much should you pay for Mac mini?
M6 Mac mini, starting at $899. 
M5 Pro Mac mini, starting at $1,699. 
Since the August 2026 update, the Mac mini is no longer the budget Mac it once was. The M6 model starts at $899, $300 more than the $599 starting price of the M4 generation.
For most people, the $899 M6 Mac mini is the model to buy. It offers more than enough performance for everyday work, browsing, media and general productivity, although the standard 16GB of unified memory and 256GB SSD may feel limiting if you plan to keep it for several years.
The base model’s 256GB SSD also deserves consideration beyond capacity. As our report on the Mac mini’s storage design explains, it uses a single NAND storage package, while the 512GB model reportedly uses two. This could affect read and write speeds, but we don’t yet have benchmarks establishing the difference. Choose 512GB if you need the extra internal space. 
If you need more demanding performance for creative work, development or larger local AI models, the M5 Pro Mac mini starts at $1,699. Upgrades can quickly push its price towards $3,000: the model we reviewed, with the full M5 Pro chip, 48GB of memory, a 1TB SSD and 10Gb Ethernet, would cost $2,899. That’s $100 more than an M5 Max Mac Studio configuration with a more powerful GPU and more ports, although that Studio has 36GB of memory rather than 48GB. Compare the configurations you actually need before choosing the mini.
Be cautious about spending heavily on Apple’s storage upgrades. External SSDs and Mac mini hubs with NVMe storage can provide considerably more capacity for less money.
For most buyers, we recommend spending around $899 on the M6 Mac mini. Move up to the M5 Pro only if you need its its stronger multicore CPU or GPU performance or significantly more memory.
Discounts are likely to appear at Amazon and other resellers over time, particularly around Prime Day in October and Black Friday in November. For now, the best bargain may be a discounted M4 Mac mini, although remaining stock is likely to be limited.
Find Apple on Amazon U.S. 
Find Apple on Amazon U.K.
Students can save $100 through Apple’s Education Store, reducing the M6 Mac mini to $799 and the M5 Pro model to $1,599. Apple’s Refurbished Store is another way to save, although it may be some time before the new M6 and M5 Pro models appear there. Read: How to get an Apple student discount at Apple’s Education Store and Should you buy a refurbished Mac. 


						

							


Reasons to buy a Mac mini

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Excellent value: The price has gone up, but the Mac mini remains one of the most versatile and cost-effective ways to enter the macOS ecosystem. Even at the new starting price of $899, the Mac mini still delivers excellent performance per dollar. That balance of price, power, and efficiency is one of the main reasons for the desktop’s growing popularity. It also offers access to professional-grade performance for significantly less cash than a similarly specced MacBook Pro.
Long software support window: The M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini will have a long usable lifespan and will receive many years of macOS updates and security support. 
Compact desktop footprint: The Mac mini’s ultra-compact 5-inch square design makes it one of the most space-efficient desktop computers available. It fits easily under monitors, in small offices, or in minimalist workstation setups. Its compact form factor also makes it particularly attractive for server racks, home labs, and multi-machine deployments. 
Retail discounts and refurbished deals: Despite already offering strong value at full price, the Mac mini is occasionally discounted by third-party retailers. If you can find a Mac mini deal – even on a M4 model with a  higher-memory configuration – we recommend taking advantage of it. The Apple Refurbished Store can offer even better value, assuming stock is available. In the past, we have seen the M4 Mac mini discounted by around $100/£100, while M4 Pro models have dropped by approximately $200/£210. If deals like these reappear, they are likely worth considering.


						

							


Reasons not to buy Mac mini
The price has gone up significantly: The Mac mini was once the undisputed budget Mac, but that is much harder to say now. The entry-level model has risen sharply in price, making it less compelling for buyers primarily looking for the cheapest way into the Mac ecosystem. At $899, the latest Mac mini is still less expensive than a MacBook or iMac, but it no longer feels like the bargain it once was.
You need to buy your own peripherals: The Mac mini is a “BYODKM” – Bring Your Own Display, Keyboard and Mouse – computer. That’s central to its appeal if you already own those accessories, but it can add substantially to the cost if you don’t. Unlike an iMac or MacBook, the Mac mini doesn’t include a display, keyboard or mouse. Buying all three can easily add hundreds of dollars to the overall price. The latest models also lack USB-A ports, so you may need adapters or a hub if you still use older accessories.
It’s not portable: The Mac mini is a desktop computer, so it isn’t suitable if you need to work in different locations. You can’t easily take it to a lecture, meeting or coffee shop in the way you can a MacBook. For students, frequent travellers or anyone who regularly works away from a desk, a laptop is likely to be the better choice.
You can’t upgrade it later: You need to choose your memory and storage carefully when you buy because neither can be upgraded afterwards. Apple’s build-to-order memory and storage upgrades can also be expensive, particularly once you start moving beyond the base configuration. This can quickly push the Mac mini into MacBook Pro or Mac Studio territory. A teardown by Expand Mac mini confirms that the M6 and M5 Pro models have their storage chips soldered to the logic board. Unlike the M4 and M4 Pro, which supported compatible third-party replacement SSD modules, the new models offer no removable module to upgrade. Choose enough internal storage when ordering or use an external SSD.
Availability could be limited: New Mac launches can sometimes bring longer delivery times for popular configurations, particularly higher-memory or build-to-order models. The M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini may suffer significant shortages due to their popularity and the shortage of components and memory.
It’s not ideal for every AI workload: Apple is increasingly positioning its Macs for AI workloads, with the M6 GPU’s Neural Accelerators and dual 16-core Neural Engine, but as our colleagues at PCWorld explain, the Mac mini has some limitations if running large local models is your main priority. The standard M6 Mac mini tops out at 32GB of unified memory, which may be restrictive for particularly large local models. The M5 Pro model offers more memory, but higher-spec configurations become expensive quickly. There is also no support for Nvidia’s CUDA platform. Many professional AI and machine-learning tools are optimized around CUDA and Nvidia GPUs, so a Windows or Linux PC with a suitable Nvidia graphics card may be faster or better supported for some workloads. For general Apple Intelligence features and lighter local AI use, however, this shouldn’t be a concern.


						

							


What to avoid when buying a Mac mini

				
					

				
			
Ida Blix




Intel: Avoid Intel-powered Mac mini models – when shopping for a refurbished Mac mini, prioritize models with Apple Silicon (M-series chips). 
Low RAM: We advise avoiding 8GB RAM models if possible, as newer generations now start with 16GB as the base standard. 
Check status: Check whether an older model is classified as vintage or obsolete. Service for vintage Macs depends on parts availability, while Apple generally ends hardware service for obsolete Macs. See: How long do Macs last.


						

							





Is Mac mini right for you?
Is the Mac mini the best choice for you? There are a number of trade-offs to consider. 


FeatureConsideration

PortabilityNot portable; requires separate monitor, keyboard, and mouse.
ConnectivityLacks USB-A ports; may require adapters for older accessories. The M5 Pro Mac mini features three Thunderbolt 5 ports, while the standard M6 model uses Thunderbolt 4. 
UpgradabilityUnified memory and internal storage cannot be upgraded by the user after purchase.

 



Who is the Mac mini best for?


UserRecommendation

Student, office work, web devBuy M6 Mac mini (or M4 if a refurbished model is available)
Creative work (photo/video)M6 for mainstream photo/video work; M5 Pro for sustained professional workloads
Local AI / LLM workloadsM5 Pro with as much unified memory as the workload requires
Existing M1/M2 Mac mini ownerConsider M6 if performance, display support, connectivity or memory limits justify upgrading
Existing M4/M4 Pro Mac mini ownerKeep it if it meets your needs; upgrade for a specific performance, memory or connectivity limitation
Intel Mac ownerBuy M6 Mac mini

 






Mac mini vs Mac Studio: Which should you buy?

				
					

				
			The Mac Studio is an even more powerful option.
Thomas Bergbold 




The choice between the Mac mini and the Mac Studio largely comes down to whether you prioritize value or maximum performance.
The M6 Mac mini offers strong value for buyers who already have a display and peripherals. The M5 Pro can also make sense for demanding work, but compare its configured price with a Mac Studio before ordering.
The Mac Studio is designed for users who need workstation-class performance. Following the discontinuation of the Mac Pro, it is now effectively Apple’s most powerful desktop. Starting at $2,499/£2,499 for the M5 Max configuration, the Mac Studio also represents the most affordable way to get a Max-series Apple Silicon chip (which starts at $4,099/£4,099 if you buy a MacBook Pro). It is well suited to professional video production, large AI models, 3D rendering, and other heavily multi-threaded or GPU-intensive workflows.
For most users, the Mac mini is a better value purchase. However, if your workloads demand high performance, more memory and a more powerful GPU, the Mac Studio is the better choice. 


						

							


Mac mini vs MacBook Neo: Which is better value?

				
					

				
			
Thomas Armbrüster




Before the introduction of the MacBook Neo, the Mac mini was Apple’s least expensive Mac. That is no longer the case – particularly now Apple has raised the price of the entry-level Mac mini from $599/£599 to $899/£899.
The MacBook Neo is now Apple’s most affordable Mac, starting at $699/£699. It is designed as an entry-level Mac and is powered by the A18 Pro chip originally used for the iPhone 16 Pro and only offers 8GB memory. The focus is on portability, battery life, and affordability rather than performance.
The Mac mini, by contrast, remains Apple’s best-value desktop Mac for users who already own a monitor, keyboard, and mouse. Thanks to its M6 and M5 Pro chips, active cooling system, and greater performance, it is better suited to demanding workloads such as coding, creative applications, multitasking, and local AI development.


						

							


Where to buy a Mac mini 
If you’re looking to buy a Mac mini, you can choose between Apple, third-party retailers and refurbished outlets.
Apple: You can buy a Mac mini directly from the Apple Store online or at an Apple retail store. 
Apple Education Store: Apple also offers discounted education pricing for eligible students and educators via its Education Store. For example, the $899 M6 Mac mini costs $799 with education pricing.
Third-Party Resellers: It’s worth checking third-party retailers as well as Apple, as stores such as Amazon and B&H frequently discount Macs. Authorized resellers and major retailers often sell the Mac mini at less than Apple’s list price.
In the U.S., retailers include:
Amazon
Best Buy
B&H Photo Video
Costco
Adorama
DataVision
In the U.K., retailers include:
Amazon
Argos
Currys
John Lewis
AO
Ebuyer
Laptops Direct
The U.K. also has Apple Premium Resellers including KRCS, iStore, Select, Albion and Jigsaw.


						

							


Should you buy a refurbished Mac mini?
A refurbished Mac mini can be an excellent way to save money, particularly if you don’t need the latest model. Discounts can be significant, although the exact saving depends on the model, configuration and seller.
The best place to start is Apple’s Refurbished Store. Apple’s refurbished Macs are fully tested, cleaned and inspected, and come with a one-year limited warranty, 90 days of technical support and eligibility for AppleCare. They are also supplied with the appropriate accessories and repackaged in a new box.
Earlier in 2026, we saw refurbished M4 Mac mini models discounted by around $90/£90, with savings also available on the M4 Pro version. However, as of September 2026, refurbished Mac mini stock is very limited. M4 models are currently unavailable, and it may be some time before the new M6 and M5 Pro models start appearing in Apple’s refurbished store.
Availability is one of the main drawbacks of buying refurbished. Stock depends on returns and trade-ins, so you may not find the exact memory or storage configuration you want. More models may become available as owners upgrade to the latest Mac minis and older machines make their way to refurbishers.
You should also be careful when buying from third-party sellers. Refurbishment standards and warranties can vary, and marketplaces may contain much older Intel-based Mac minis. We generally wouldn’t recommend those models now unless the price is exceptionally low, as Apple silicon Mac minis offer much better performance and will receive software support for longer.
We’ve found Amazon particularly worth checking carefully. Refurbished stock can be dominated by Mac minis from 2020 or earlier, and we’ve even seen discontinued configurations listed for more than their original selling price. Always check the model year, specification and price of an equivalent new Mac before buying.
Buying refurbished is generally safer than buying second hand from a private seller. A reputable refurbished Mac should have been inspected and tested and will usually include a warranty and returns policy. A privately sold Mac may offer neither, and there is also a risk of Activation Lock if the previous owner hasn’t properly removed the Mac from their Apple Account.
Where to buy a refurbished Mac mini
U.S.: Amazon, Back Market, Best Buy, GainSaver, Mac of All Trades and Refurb.me.
U.K.: Affordable Mac, Amazon, Back Market, Hoxton Macs, MacFinder, Mac4Sale and MusicMagpie.
Read our guide to the pros and cons of buying refurbished Macs. We also have recommendations of the best places to buy a refurbished Mac.

title: Apple Intelligence Taking Up 30GB+ on Some Macs Running macOS 27
content:
After you install macOS 27 Golden Gate, Apple automatically downloads a multi-gigabyte AI model to your Mac the next time it's connected to the internet. Unlike previous versions of macOS, you can't prevent it. Siri AI, and by extension Apple Intelligence, are now a mandatory part of your system.


For macOS 27 Golden Gate, Apple says the latest Apple Intelligence features require up to 14GB of on-device storage on Macs with an M3 chip or later and at least 12GB of unified memory, and up to 8GB of storage for other Apple Intelligence-enabled Macs. But in our experience, AI model storage allocation appears to be considerably higher on some Macs than others.

MacRumors saw 20.67GB handed over for Apple Intelligence, according to the Storage section in System Settings. ArsTechnica recorded an even higher figure of 22.42GB on an M3 MacBook Air after a fresh installation of macOS 27.0 beta 7. Both of these systems will be using Apple's AFM 3 Core Advanced on-device model, which requires an M3-or-newer Mac with 12GB or more of RAM.

ArsTechnica reported the same screen showed around 14GB on an M1 MacBook Air and a MacBook Neo, and yet both of these models fall into a category for which Apple lists a requirement of up to 8GB.

shared a screenshot from the macOS 27 Release Candidate showing Apple Intelligence gobbled up 30.16GB on their machine. Another user quoted 24.35GB for Apple Intelligence after installing macOS 27 on a MacBook Pro with M3 Pro chip.


  

    Device

Up to 14GB

Figures taken from Apple's support document

Apple's support document does not explain whether its "up to 14GB" requirement is directly comparable with the Apple Intelligence "Storage" category in System Settings, or why some Macs display substantially higher numbers. (For what it's worth, we haven't seen the same ballooning figures on iPhones and iPads running iOS 27 and iPadOS 27.)

because of AI, the irony of this situation cannot be lost. It doesn't make it any less frustrating, though.

System Settings ➝ General ➝ Storage by clicking the information button beside macOS. Let us know your findings in the comments.

title: New Mac Mini Has Two Storage Downsides, Including Unremovable SSD
content:
As confirmed by the website "Expand Mac mini," NAND storage in the new Mac mini models with the M6 and M5 Pro chips is soldered to the logic board, whereas the previous models with the M4 and M4 Pro chips have removable storage that can be upgraded.


In other words, the new Mac mini does not support aftermarket storage upgrades.

"Expand Mac mini" offers plug-and-play SSD modules that are functionally equivalent to Apple's proprietary modules, yet hundreds of dollars cheaper. As a result, customers were able to save a significant amount of money by configuring their Mac mini with the minimum 256GB capacity that was available on Apple's online store and later installing a higher-capacity aftermarket module. With the new models, that is no longer possible.

"We will keep looking for an opening, but support for the M6 and M5 Pro now looks unlikely," the "Expand Mac mini" website said, in a blog post.

Mac mini models with the M1 chip and M2/M2 Pro chips also had NAND soldered to the logic board, so the M4/M4 Pro configurations having removable storage has proven to be a one-off exception for now. Apple has not commented on the reversal.

AAPL Ch.'s testing with Blackmagic's Disk Speed Test benchmark tool.

Fortunately, even with 256GB of storage, it appears that the new Mac mini has meaningfully faster SSD speeds compared to the previous 256GB model.

title: OpenAI's New GPT-6 Sol and Luna Models Bring Astra Improvements to Cheaper Tiers
content:
OpenAI today launched GPT–6 Sol and GPT–6 Luna, two new models that follow GPT–6 Astra. OpenAI says the new models were developed using methods similar to Astra's for improvements in professional work, factuality, coding, computer use, and alignment.


GPT–6 Sol is for everyday work, and it costs less than Astra. GPT–6 Luna is an even cheaper model. Luna is optimized for fast responses and higher volume, while Sol has more reasoning capability.

The new models outperform their predecessors on OpenAI's benchmark tests, and GPT–6 Sol makes "about half as many mistakes" as GPT–5.6 Sol. GPT–6 Sol shows improvements in coding and computer use compared to GPT–5.6 Sol, and it matches or beats Claude Fable 5.1 scores on some benchmarks.

Opus 5.5 model today that outperforms Astra on some coding and knowledge work benchmarks.

GPT–6 Sol and Luna are adopting the improved communication style OpenAI introduced with Astra for simplified conversations with less jargon and fewer low-value details. Answers should be slightly shorter without losing substance, and the new models have lower rates of misleading claims about their coding work in OpenAI's alignment testing.

OpenAI is lowering token prices for Sol and Luna compared to their 5.6 counterparts, and prompt caching has been improved. OpenAI says agents will reuse more context, respond faster, and get 90 percent discounts on cached input-token reads.

GPT–6 Sol is priced at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, down by half. GPT–6 Luna costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, down from $0.20 and $1.20, respectively. GPT–6 Sol costs half as much per token as Opus 5.5, but Anthropic says Opus 5.5 uses fewer tokens per task than Opus 5, so it's not a straight comparison.

title: Apple’s new Beats headphones are AirPods Max for athletes
content:
Macworld





The newest Beats over-ear headphones are here, and as evidenced by the many leaks, are made for athletes. Specifically, athletes who liked the idea of AirPods Max but passed on them because they were too heavy, too drab, or, most importantly, too expensive.
First, the price: Beats 360 are $350, significantly less than the $449 AirPods Max. For that price, you’re getting much of what Apple’s high-end headphones offer: Active Noise Cancellation, Transparency mode, Personalized Spatial Audio with dynamic head tracking, and Adaptive EQ. iPhone users will also get one-touch pairing, Automatic Switching, Audio Sharing, Find My support, and hands-free “Hey Siri.”
While Beats says they have “the best acoustics from Beats to date, as well as the best noise cancellation yet from Beats,” they don’t have some features AirPods users might miss. Since they have a custom-designed proprietary Beats chip rather than an H2, you’re not getting AirPods features such as Live Translation, Hearing Protection, and Conversation Boost.
However, if you can live without those features, Beats 360 are everything AirPods Max aren’t. Most notably, they’re very light, weighing just 295 grams, versus AirPods Max’s 386 grams. The cushions are available in one of two options: performance knit for workouts or ultralush for longer listening sessions. They also come in a variety of bright colors–Black, Cloud (off-white), Pink, and Sky (blue)–that are encouraged to be mixed and matched with different cushions, which are available in their own set of colors and cost $50 each, with a special launch price of $10.
While AirPods Max aren’t rated for water resistance, Beats 360 have IPX4 sweat and water resistance, making them very gym friendly. They also feature on-device controls for controlling music. You get 32 hours of battery life, about 50 percent more than AirPods Max.
You can order Beats 360 on the Apple website, Beats website, or through Amazon and other third-party retailers for shipping beginning Thursday.
creator: Macworld

Opus 5.5 is comparable to Mythos 5.1 in biology and cybersecurity, so Anthropic is launching it with safeguards similar to those on Fable 5.1. On benchmarks shared by Anthropic, Opus 5.5 surpassed Fable 5.1 on agentic coding, knowledge work, computer use, visual chart recognition, and multidisciplinary reasoning. Anthropic says the model communicates more naturally than prior models, putting important information at the front of a response so it's easier to understand at a glance. It is less likely to use jargon or idiosyncratic phrases, and it follows the writing rules it's given.

title: How to clear System Data on Mac and free up storage space
content:
Macworld





If your Mac is warning that you are running out of storage, you need room for a macOS update, or your Mac simply seems to be slowing down, you may have looked at the large chunk of storage labelled System Data and wondered if you can safely delete it to save space on your Mac. 
Low storage can cause all kinds of problems on a Mac – you might see warnings that your startup disk is almost full, struggle to install macOS updates, notice performance slowdowns, or in extreme cases even have trouble starting up your Mac. Maintaining at least 10% of your total storage as free space is generally recommended to ensure your Mac continues to run smoothly.
So what exactly is System Data, why can it grow so large, and is it safe to remove anything from it? The answer is yes — at least some of it. Just beware that deleting some files from System Data could seriously damage your installation of macOS, so we recommend that you back up your Mac before deleting anything, just in case!
In this guide, we’ll explain what’s included in System Data, why it can take up so many gigabytes, and the simple steps you can take to delete System Data and reclaim space on your Mac. If you aren’t sure how to see how much disk space your Mac has read: How to check how much disk space you have.

What is System Data on Mac?
System Data on Mac is a broad storage category that serves as a catch-all for various files that do not fit into standard classifications like Applications, Documents, or Photos. 
While the specific contents vary for every user, System Data typically includes the following types of files:
Caches and Logs: System and application caches designed to help your Mac run more smoothly.
Temporary Files: Data created during daily use that is often intended to be deleted automatically by the OS.
Backups: Local Time Machine snapshots and iOS backups.
Plug-ins and Extensions: Support files for various applications.
Disk Images: Downloaded .dmg files used for upgrading apps or macOS.
App Leftovers: Bits of data that remain on the drive even after the main application has been deleted.
System Data, System, macOS and Other 

				
					

				
			
Find out what’s taking up all the space.

Foundry




Apple has changed how this storage category is labeled in different versions of macOS.   
In macOS Big Sur (macOS 11) and earlier, much of this storage was grouped under a category called “Other.” In macOS Catalina (macOS 10.15) and the subsequent Big Sur, there was also a separate category labeled “System,” which included core macOS files and other system-related data.

				
					

				
			Older versions of macOS labeled certain types of storage as System or Other. 
Starting with macOS Monterey (macOS 12), Apple reorganized these categories, replacing much of the System/Other terminology with “System Data,” while also introducing a separate “macOS” category for the operating system itself.
In newer versions of macOS, including Sequoia and Golden Gate, the category continues to appear as “System Data” alongside the separate “macOS” category.


						

							


Why is System Data so large? 

				
					

				
			
System Data was over 100GB. Is that a record? 

Foundry




System Data is intended to be managed automatically by macOS, but it can occasionally balloon to an unexpected size, sometimes taking up more than 100GB of storage. This is particularly problematic on Macs with smaller 256GB SSDs, where System Data can unexpectedly consume nearly half of the available space. 
This happened to us when macOS started temporarily storing update-related files inside System Data as well as reindexing iCloud and Spotlight files while preparing to install an update to macOS. That was when we concluded that a 256GB SSD is too small for a Mac.
System Data can grow as apps and macOS accumulate caches, logs, temporary files and other support data. The main cause varies from Mac to Mac.
Key factors that drive the growth of System Data include:
Streaming Caches: One of the biggest culprits is streaming high-quality music and video. While downloaded media is indexed separately, streamed content creates large caches to ensure smooth playback, which are categorized as System Data.
Browser and App Caches: Safari and other browsers store website data to speed up loading times. Over time, these caches can grow to several gigabytes.
Messaging Data: If you frequently send and receive high-resolution images or videos via apps like Messages, the cached attachments can significantly inflate system storage.
System Maintenance: Files such as Time Machine snapshots, iOS backups stored on a computer, and macOS update installers often reside in this category. 
The impact of local AI models on System Data
A new and increasingly common cause of large System Data storage is the rise of local artificial intelligence features. Modern operating systems, browsers, and apps now download sizeable AI models so they can perform tasks directly on your device rather than relying entirely on cloud processing.
These local AI models can have a significant impact on macOS storage because the model files themselves are often several gigabytes in size.
Features such as Apple Intelligence, offline transcription tools, coding assistants, and image-generation apps may all store large language models, caches, and other AI assets locally on your Mac. Many of these files are saved in hidden Library folders, caches, containers, or developer directories, so they don’t appear in obvious categories like Applications or Documents. Instead, they can dramatically increase the amount of storage attributed to System Data.
AI workloads can also create large temporary files, caches, and logs while models are running, further increasing storage usage over time.
Apple Intelligence adds to your Mac’s storage requirements. For macOS 27 Golden Gate, Apple lists up to 14GB of on-device storage for Macs with M3 or later and at least 12GB of unified memory, and up to 8GB for other compatible Macs. These are storage requirements for Apple Intelligence – not an indication that all of that space will appear under System Data.


						

							


Is it safe to delete System Data on a Mac?

				
					

				
			Beware: Deleting is permanent.
Foundry




Apple does not provide a simple Delete button for System Data because the category contains many files required for macOS to function properly. If it were possible to remove everything included in System Data, it could seriously damage your installation of macOS.
However, some files classed as System Data are non-essential and can be safely removed to free up space. These may include certain caches, logs, temporary files, old backups, and unused application support files.
That said, you should proceed carefully and only delete files if you are confident you understand what they are. Removing the wrong files can lead to application errors, system instability, or, in extreme cases, prevent your Mac from starting up properly.
In particular, you should avoid deleting:
Operating System Files: Core macOS files required for the system to run.
System Caches: These help macOS and apps run efficiently, and deleting the wrong cache files can cause problems.
Hidden System Files: Apple hides many critical files specifically to prevent accidental damage.


						

							


What System Data files can I safely delete? 
If you need to free up storage space on your Mac, there are several types of System Data files that are generally safe to remove.
Old Time Machine Snapshots: Local Time Machine snapshots can sometimes consume large amounts of storage space. These are temporary backups stored on your Mac and can usually be safely deleted if you already have backups saved elsewhere.
iPhone and iPad backups: Old iOS and iPadOS backups stored on your Mac can take up many gigabytes. If you no longer need them, they can be safely removed.
Application caches: While you should avoid deleting core system caches, clearing caches created by individual apps is usually safe. Keep in mind that many apps will simply recreate these files over time.
Disk image files (.dmg): Downloaded installer files for apps you have already installed are often left behind in the Downloads folder and can safely be deleted once they are no longer needed.
Temporary files and logs: Some temporary files and log files generated by apps and macOS can be removed, especially if they are old or unusually large. However, proceed with caution, as some of these files are necessary for system performance and stability.
Unused AI model files: Modern versions of macOS and some third-party apps may download large AI models for on-device features. Don’t manually delete Apple Intelligence files from system folders. For third-party AI tools, remove unused models through the app’s own controls. 
We’ll explain how to manually remove files from each of these categories below. We’ll also recommend some apps that can help you with this. 


						

							


Best apps to delete System Data on a Mac
If you don’t feel confident deleting these files manually, you may prefer to use a dedicated cleanup tool to reduce the risk of accidentally damaging macOS or deleting important system files. 
There are several specialized cleaning utilities specifically designed to identify and remove System Data files including large caches, logs, and temporary files that are often difficult to locate manually. These tools can help identify potentially removable files, but review their recommendations before deleting anything.
